Ground mismatch: WAS are run-first (38% pass when leading) into a NYG front that bleeds 142 rush yds/game and 0.53 RB1 rushing scores. Jacory Croskey-Merritt is a centerpiece — and the game script only feeds him.

The WAS host the NYG as favorites of 2.5, with the total set at 48.5 — a market that implies a WAS 26–23 scoreline. Running the game forward from that baseline, we expect a contest that spends roughly 26% of its snaps with WAS in front, 39% within one score, and 34% with WAS chasing. That distribution is the engine of everything below: game state is what turns a team's tendencies into a specific player's workload, so before we get to individuals it's worth being explicit about how this game is likely to be played.

This is a coin-flip script. With only 2.5 points separating them, neither team projects to spend much time in a blowout state — most of the game lives in the 'close' bucket, where play-calling stays balanced and usage tracks each player's established role rather than being distorted by score. In tight games the stars on both sides see their normal, dependable workloads, and there is less garbage-time leakage to backups.

The Key Matchups

Jayden Daniels adds rushing value — he scrambles on 6.7% of dropbacks, live for rush-yard and anytime-TD props.

Efficiency edge to WAS — a 47% success-rate offense against a NYG defense that allows 46% — points should come.

Malik Nabers draws a plus matchup — WAS concede 68 yds/game to WR1s (league ~58), and NYG funnel 29% of targets his way. A rec-yards spot.

Touchdown Board

Theo Johnson is a live anytime-TD dart — WAS are leaky to tight ends in the end zone (0.35 TE TDs/game vs ~0.24).

Malik Nabers carries TD equity — WAS surrender 0.51 WR1 receiving scores a game.

WAS — a run-heavy offense

WAS are one of the league's more run-committed offenses: on early downs while leading, they pass just 38% of the time, against a league average of 44% — a genuine clock-bleeding identity, not noise (it holds after shrinking their sample toward the league).

Jacory Croskey-Merritt (11 carries, 49 yards) projects to his baseline workload — no strong script push either way in a close game.

Terry McLaurin projects for 6 targets and 51 yards, in line with his established role in a script that neither inflates nor suppresses the pass.

Underneath, Chig Okonkwo (TE, 5 targets, 34 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

NYG — a balanced offense

NYG are a balanced offense — their run/pass split by game state tracks the league closely (42% pass when leading vs 44% average), so their players' usage is driven more by role than by any strong situational lean.

Tyrone Tracy Jr. (12 carries, 54 yards) projects to his baseline workload — no strong script push either way in a close game.

Malik Nabers projects for 8 targets and 58 yards, in line with his established role in a script that neither inflates nor suppresses the pass.

Underneath, Theo Johnson (TE, 6 targets, 42 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

What to watch

The single biggest swing factor is availability — use the injury tool in the sidebar to mark anyone out; a starter's absence doesn't just remove his line, it redistributes his targets and carries to specific teammates, and the report and projections rebuild around it. Beyond that: if this game breaks toward the projected 2-point margin, the garbage-time backups (the ◆-flagged rows below) are where soft lines and real edge tend to appear — those depth players get fed in blowouts, and the market is slowest to price them.

This preview and the projections below regenerate through the week as injuries, weather and line moves update the inputs.
